persona: Merchandiser and buyer for a curated online shop (formerly a museum store), the sceptic: would someone pay $50, does it stand out from generic art and souvenir tees, would it photograph well.

designs.why: Crisp, bold, high-contrast woodcut line that prints cleanly and photographs well, and the head and armour detail rewards a close look. 'DRAWN FROM A RUMOR.' is the reason to buy: it turns the most over-merchandised public-domain animal in museum shops into a witty, knowing piece. I'd stock it at $50. Docked because the Dürer rhino is very familiar, and the cut-away rear reads at a glance as a blunt slab on the left rather than a deliberate crop.
designs.fix: Make the crop look intentional: either square the cut off with a clean ruled plate edge or frame line, or pull the animal right so the cut edge sits flush with the print boundary. The caption could also be set a touch tighter, so it locks up with the 1515 RHINOCERVS heading as one composition.
designs.title: Drawn from a Rumor

designs.why: Real provenance (Hooke, 1665) and engraving-quality line that prints crisply. The plate letters (K, L, M) add authenticity, and the caption gives the buyer a story to tell, which is exactly what sells a $50 tee. Weaknesses: the close crop loses the famous whole-flea silhouette, so from 3 m it reads as a dark armoured lump with a small head, the straight cut along the left edge looks like a mistake rather than a choice, and the thin trailing legs leave the lower half airy.
designs.fix: Show the whole Hooke flea (the iconic full silhouette), scaled to fill the print area, and keep the caption under it; at minimum, recrop so the head and eye sit nearer the centre and the cut edge reads as intentional.
designs.title: Nobody Had Looked

overall: The rhino wins clearly. The art is strong and well known, and the caption is a real hook that sets it apart from the usual museum-shop Dürer tee. The oak and fox den is pleasant but generic, and its tonal halftone softens exactly the part a customer would zoom in on.
